newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clinton honors Mexico's boy heroes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton honors Mexico's boy heroes.

text.p: No words were spoken and the ceremony was simple, but U.S. President Bill Clinton's homage to Mexico's Boy Heroes on Tuesday spoke volumes about the rocky history of U.S.-Mexico relations.

Clinton laid a wreath of flowers with the American flag at the base of the Mexico City monument, which celebrates six teenage Mexican cadets who died while U.S. invaders seized the historic Chapultepec Castle 150 years ago.

Two rows of military cadets watched as Clinton, on a three-day state visit, and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo stood silently at the foot of a hill where legend says one of the cadets leaped to his death draped in the Mexican flag rather than surrender to U.S. soldiers.

The ceremony was seen as an act of respect by the U.S. leader for the memory of the 1847 Mexican-American war, after which Mexico ceded to its northern neighbour nearly half its territory, including a large swath of land from west Texas to Colorado to California.

Earlier, Clinton said he thought it was appropriate for him to visit the monument, which is a regular stop for foreign dignitaries in Mexico and is known as the "Altar de la Patria," or Altar to the Nation.
"We hope to heal the wounds of war," Clinton told reporters.

The New York Times reported on Tuesday that U.S. officials had been wary of scheduling a stop for Clinton at a monument that stands as a stark reminder to Mexicans of long-standing domination by their huge northern neighbour.
The Ninos Heroes are mandatory material for Mexican schoolchildren and their monument is considered among the most important in Mexico's nationalist pantheon.

Passions among Mexicans are still aroused by talk of the war, and the stars and stripes a common object of abuse. Shortly before Clinton arrived on Monday, a group of leftist protesters burned the U.S. flag in front of the embassy in Mexico City.

Clinton has in other parts of his visit also tried to smooth over some more recent rough spots in Mexico-U.S. ties, including issues of drug trafficking and illegal immigration between Mexico and the United States.
Clinton's brief visit to the monument evoked memories of a similar act by President Harry Truman half a century earlier.

On the last day of Truman's three-day visit, the first ever by a U.S. President to Mexico City, he made an unscheduled stop at the monument and paid homage to the Boy Heroes who had died 100 years earlier.
A contingent of blue-uniformed cadets stood guard as Truman placed a floral wreath, according to newspaper reports from the time. A few cadets wept silently.

"With one simple, unheralded gesture, he did more to improve Mexican-American relations than had any President in a century. Within hours, as word spread, he was a hero," historian David McCullough wrote in his biography of Truman.
